newsitem.title: GUAM: U.S. lifts Lebanon travel ban. [CORRECTED 11:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. lifts Lebanon travel ban. [CORRECTED 11:40 GMT]

text.p: The United States Wednesday lifted a 12-year-old (Corrects from 10-year-old) ban on U.S. citizens visiting Lebanon after receiving pledges from the government in Beirut to do more to fight terrorism.
But Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in announcing the decision, said Lebanon remains a dangerous place and she issued what she called a "stern" warning urging Americans not to travel there.
She and other U.S. officials claimed the decision was based on a legal interpretation of U.S. law and not on political factors, like its potential impact on Middle East peace.
"I have decided to let it expire," Albright said of the ban that Lebanon and the politically active community of Lebanese- Americans had long sought to revoke.

Speaking to reporters travelling with her from Singapore, she said she acted after Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri promised her in a telephone call to greatly increase cooperation in fighting terrorism.

A special Lebanese envoy is due in Washington this week to work on this issue and Hariri also has promised to try to get his parliament to ratify by October the last of ten conventions committing Lebanon to work with the United States in hostage-taking cases, she said.
President (Bill) Clinton met Hariri last October and U.S. officials believe the Lebanese leader has become more personally involved in the local security situation.
The ban was imposed in 1985 (Corrects from 1987) during the Lebanese civil war and after Moslem zealots hijacked a TWA airliner to Beirut and killed an American passenger.
Albright said the latest U.S. government assessment of security risk in Lebanon concluded the threat had diminished in recent years and was at an even lower level during the past six months.

Nevertheless, she insisted this was not to meant to be interpreted as a sign she encouraged Americans to visit Lebanon. "I still believe Lebanon is a dangerous place," she said. She reserves the right to reimpose the ban in the future.
The ban is not watertight as it bars American citizens only from using their U.S. passports to visit Lebanon. Dual citizens can still use their Lebanese passports.

The travel ban has been widely ignored, especially by some 40,000 Lebanese-American dual nationals who visit Beirut each year, but Lebanese officials say it continues to put a damper on business relations between the two countries.
Secretaries of state review the ban every six months and Albright faced that deadline on Thursday, prompting the action she announced on Wednesday.
There are many places in the world where it is dangerous for Americans to travel but where the U.S. government does not impose legal restrictions on doing so.
"I don't believe we should be pushing Americans to break the law," Albright said.

The ban was based on a judgment that Americans faced a serious security threat in Lebanon, especially from pro-Iranian Hizbollah guerrillas who remain at large there. The claim had been disputed by the Lebanese government.
Lifting the ban puts Lebanon in a category with countries like Sudan, Afghanistan, Algeria, Colombia and Iran, instead of bracketing it with Iraq and Libya, to which travel is banned.

Since Lebanon's civil war ended in 1991, U.S. leaders have several times been tempted to end the ban in order to increase Lebanon's independence from its patron Syria and boost the standing of Hariri, who is well-liked in Washington.
Albright said Wedensday: "In the long-run, what we'd like to see is an independent Lebanon."

In makaing its decision, the administration has remained haunted by memories of the 1980s, when 241 U.S. servicemen died in a 1983 suicide truck bombing at a Marine base in Beirut and dozens of other Americans died in two bomb attacks on embassy buildings.
Still other Americans were held hostage in Lebanon for years in the late 1980s by Iranian-backed guerrillas.
Lebanese officials contend their country is now safer than many that Americans are not banned from visiting. They have portrayed the ban as U.S. pressure on Lebanon to join peace talks with Israel.
